![][image1]

relationships are hard—apparently.

not in the sense that I can’t invest or commit. I can.

that’s the problem.

I’m trying to figure out how little I can ask for—without feeling like I’m losing something.

situationship? easy. light. no *“this is real”* panic— just enough presence to keep things moving.

casual? also viable. proximity, warmth, conversation. coffee after, like nothing means anything.

back burner?

now we’re getting interesting.

not needed, not chosen—just… available.

I have my own life. you have yours. we intersect when convenient.

it sounds healthy when you say it slowly. like I’m being understanding. like I’m giving space. like I’m not asking for too much.

but I think—I’m just negotiating.

lowering the terms. adjusting the language. reframing the loss.

until it becomes something I can tolerate.

because the alternative is simple—and I don’t like it.

either I step away, or I go all in.

and I already know—if given the chance—I would abandon all sense of reason just to be with you.

so instead, I sit here… trying to design a version of this where I don’t have to find out.

![][image2]

I treated it like currency.

Like if I accumulated enough of it,

I could justify being here.

Not just useful—

but necessary.

Not just capable—

but chosen.

It works in smaller systems.

It builds.

Optimizes.

Stabilizes.

It makes me someone you can rely on.

But reliability isn’t desire.

And desire isn’t meaning.

So I kept sharpening it.

As if omnipotence

could substitute for being chosen.

As if precision

could answer something larger.

It doesn’t.

Because competence only responds to problems.

And existence… isn’t one.

So I’m left with this:

capable enough to function.

not sufficient enough to explain.

And still asking—

not why I wasn’t chosen.

But why I’m here at all.

No answer.

Just refinement.

I saw a post about stickers—

not calling anyone out or anything—

and it might be the most charming thing I’ve seen all day.

because somewhere behind all the philosophy and overthinking,

I’m usually the one who uses them immediately

sticks them anywhere—

right place, wrong place, this place, that place—

just so they don’t sit there untouched

and I can kind of picture you

with a small hoard of perfectly kept things

a quiet little collection

you never quite use

and there’s something about that

that feels… nice

so now I’m just here—

liking the way you keep things

while I keep ruining perfectly good stickers on purpose

![][image4]

I call it awareness—

this distance I keep from my own suffering.

The way I can step outside of it just enough to study its shape.

Not avoid it—

refine it.

There’s a kind of craft to it now.

The pacing.

The restraint.

What I let linger, what I cut before it dulls.

As if pain, left untuned, risks becoming meaningless.

I adjust it.

Quiet the excess.

Sharpen what remains.

It begins to resemble something intentional—

not raw experience, but composition.

I tell myself this is control.

That I’ve mastered distance—

that observation is not the same as participation.

But the line doesn’t hold.

Because the more I refine it, the more it feels authored.

Not imposed on me—

but sustained.

A kind of mastery that doesn’t end the suffering—

only makes it… precise.

And precision has its own danger.

It makes things worth returning to.

Worth continuing.

Not because I need it—

but because I’ve learned how to.

![][image5]

They say men think about the Roman Empire more than they admit.

I don’t.

Not in the way they mean it.

Because Rome is not interesting for how long it lasted.

It’s interesting because it ended—  and never really did.

She wasn’t something I admired from a distance.

She was something I was built inside of.

We were not stable.  We were not careful.

We were kids trying to understand things we didn’t have the language for yet—  love, care, attachment—  learning it from each other like it would be enough.

It wasn’t.

It was chaos in a way that didn’t feel meaningful at the time—  just necessary.

The kind you survive first  and understand later.

She abandoned me.

That should have been the end.

It wasn’t.

Because nothing actually disappeared.

It just… changed form.

She is in how I write.

In the music I return to  without thinking.

In the way I measure time—  what I keep,  what I let go of.

In coffee.  In tea.

In things that no longer have anything to do with her.

Rome didn’t disappear.

It became the structure everything else was built on.

Language.  Law.  Architecture.

You don’t think about it—  you just live in it.

It still exists.

Just not for me.

I don’t think about her all the time.

But everything I think with—  was shaped there.

So no—

she’s not my Roman Empire.

I’m just living in what’s left of it.

![][image6]

1. **Break your heart.**  
   **Yes—on purpose.**  
   Find something or someone you love and don’t negotiate with it. No half-steps, no contingency plans, no quiet distance you can retreat to when it gets inconvenient.  
   Take it whole—  
   like a good girl—  
   and don’t flinch when it asks something of you.  
   Don’t bargain. Don’t pace yourself. Don’t pretend you’re above it.  
   This is a terrible idea.  
   Genuinely.  
   It will cost you—sleep, time, pride. Maybe the thing itself. Maybe more than that.  
   But that’s the price of finding out how much of yourself you can actually put on the table without disappearing.  
   Most people never learn that.  
   They stay intact.  
   Careful.  
   Emotionally well-behaved.  
   And permanently unsure if anything they felt was real.  
   A broken heart, at least, answers the question.  
2. **Steel yourself for competence.**  
   **Not as a personality trait—but as infrastructure.**  
   Doubt does not care how insightful you are. It is not impressed.  
   It wants proof. Repeated, boring, undeniable proof that you can actually do things.  
   So build. Obsess a little. Overdo it.  
   Become slightly insufferable about it.  
   No—you are not going to become competent by curating an identity.  
   You are not a “finance guy” because you own a quarter-zip.  
   You are not in tech because you tweet about AI.  
   You are not disciplined because you wake up early twice a week.  
   Competence is quieter than that.  
   It shows up in what still works  
   when you are tired, distracted, and no one is watching.  
   Yes—maybe it’s overcompensation.  
   Good.  
   At least you chose something useful to overcompensate with instead of whatever personality trait you were going to cling to instead.  
   Because one day you’re going to be tired, cornered, and very close to folding—  
   and competence will be the only thing in the room still functioning.  
   It shows up.  
   Unlike your motivation.  
   Unlike your feelings.  
   Unlike whoever you were texting.  
3. **Assume nothing will work—**  
   **and continue anyway.**  
   Not as defeat. As calibration.  
   Effort does not guarantee outcomes.  
   It never did.  
   Things will fail.  
   Not dramatically—just enough to waste your time.  
   Timing will miss.  
   People will leave.  
   Plans will collapse right when they start to look real.  
   None of this is unusual.  
   You just expected it to go differently.  
   If you need things to work in order to keep going,  
   you’ve already lost.  
   So remove the condition.  
   You move because you decided to move.  
   You continue because stopping does nothing.  
   It won’t feel good.  
   It won’t feel meaningful.  
   That’s not a problem.  
   What matters is this:  
   It holds.  
   When motivation drops.  
   When outcomes don’t show.  
   When nothing validates the effort.  
   It still holds.  
   And that is the difference.  
   Not intelligence.  
   Not talent.  
   Not luck.  
   Stability.  
   In a decade full of variables—  
   that’s the only advantage that compounds.  
   I know—this all sounds a little arrogant.  
   It is.  
   It’s what’s left after doing everything right  
   and realizing the world doesn’t owe you a result for it.

![][image7]

Let me dismantle the metaphysical implications of her laugh.

At baseline, laughter is nothing.

A pressure fluctuation in air. Oscillatory patterns moving through a medium, registered by a biological receiver as signal. Frequency, amplitude, decay. No inherent meaning. Just physics mistaken for experience. Interchangeable. Replicable. Disposable.

Reduce it far enough and it collapses into mechanism.

So whatever significance it carries isn’t intrinsic—it’s assigned.

Which is where relational economics comes in. Laughter operates as social currency: a marker of ease, alignment, shared context. It signals safety, mutual calibration, lowered friction between two systems.

That’s its function.

That’s why it matters.

Except that explanation doesn’t hold.

Not here.

Because those conditions are common. Replaceable. If meaning were purely relational, then any sufficiently compatible input should produce the same response.

This didn’t.

Which introduces the first implication:

It wasn’t important because laughter has value.

It was important because it was hers.

Not as preference. Not as sentiment.

As constraint.

The variable collapsed into a constant.

And that’s already a problem.

Because once a system privileges a specific source over equivalent inputs, it stops operating on general rules. It begins to orient. Structure becomes singular. Substitution fails.

Which leads to the second implication.

It bypassed the system.

No evaluation. No comparison. No delay.

It didn’t enter as data—it entered as fit.

Immediate. Frictionless. The kind of integration that doesn’t register as foreign, so it never triggers resistance.

That shouldn’t happen.

Anything that integrates that cleanly is either already known—

or already decided.

And I don’t remember deciding.

So this stops being about perception.

It becomes a problem of ontology.

If a signal can arrive and be recognized as correct without mediation, then the criteria for correctness must exist prior to the moment. Not constructed—preconfigured. Not learned—already there.

Or—

formed so quickly it only appears that way.

Which means the system isn’t generating meaning.

It’s revealing it.

Or collapsing fast enough that the difference disappears.

Not building alignment—

finding it.

And that’s where this turns.

Because if that’s true, then the response wasn’t spontaneous.

It was recognition.

And recognition implies precedent.

Something in me already knew the shape of that laugh before I heard it.

Already had a place for it.

Not metaphorically.

Structurally.

Or something in me made the space the moment it arrived—

and did it so seamlessly it registered as memory.

Either way, the effect is the same.

It fit.

Exactly.

Not close.

Not approximate.

Exact enough that comparison never activated.

And I didn’t choose that.

I didn’t evaluate it.

I didn’t even get the chance to reject it.

It arrived—

and something in me closed around it

like it had been missing.

**Her laugh didn’t mean anything.**

**It just fit in a place I don’t remember making.**

![][image8]

I am not good.

I can resemble it, convincingly enough—

but let’s not mistake vows

for nature.

I tend to… arrange people, I suppose.

A little structure here,

a steadier footing there—

something that passes for direction.

They improve.

Stabilize.

Stay.

And I suppose that’s what matters.

Though I can’t say I feel much of it.

I watch them settle into something more functional,

more coherent—

as if they had always been meant to be that way.

And when they are…

they grow quiet.

Predictable.

Less interesting.

Yet still—

they look at me with that same peculiar softness.

As if I had given them something.

As if I were kind.

I am merely letting them

lick grace from my fingers—

and they take it for something far more sacred than it is.

It would almost be forgivable…

if it weren’t so consistent.

Because once is a chance.

Twice is coincidence.

But this?

This is pattern.

And so I begin to wonder—

whether the fault lies in what I do,

or in how easily it is received.

Because I do not free anyone.

I only… reshape.

Gently, perhaps.

Effectively, certainly.

Until they resemble something better—

according to me.

And somehow,

that continues to pass for virtue.

![][image9]

It’s not that difficult to move on.

That’s the assumption.

Proven, time and time again, by almost everyone.

That given enough time everything rearranges.

That what was once directed to one place

can be redirected elsewhere.

The capacity remains.

It simply requires a new object.

Perhaps that applies to me.

That I chose to move

no matter how heretical it felt.

That the capacity stayed.

Not only stayed, but refined. Expanded. Improved.

Yet the notion of loving another

is of far greater difficulty

than anything time had promised.

It is simple, yes—

to choose, repeatedly, day by day.

To follow through.

To carry life forward with whatever presents itself,

no matter how small that experience may be.

And so it is not a matter of effort.

But I cannot look at them

with the same gaze

I have for you.

And that does not change.

![][image10]

I. The Offering

I offer you my heart, dearest.

Break it, if you please.

This is not a question of worth. Nor sanity.

It is a statement of character.

I know you—well enough to understand the outcome.

And still, here.

The most fragile part of me, placed willingly in the hands most likely to destroy it.

For it is the only thing I have that has not been shaped for survival.

The only thing that has not learned restraint.

A devil such as I has very little left that can be called sacred.

This is one of them.

And I offer it without expectation of mercy.

⸻

II. Dissection

What is being expressed here is often mistaken for devotion.

It is not.

It is a deliberate act of exposure in the presence of known consequence.

The speaker is not unaware. There is no illusion being maintained. The outcome is understood in advance, and that understanding does not prevent the act—it defines it.

This reframes the gesture entirely.

It is no longer about attachment, nor longing, nor even reciprocity. It becomes a question of character: whether the capacity to offer something unguarded persists, even when its destruction is all but certain.

The distinction matters.

Most forms of vulnerability are conditional. They rely on the possibility of preservation, on the hope—however faint—that what is given will be held with care. Remove that possibility, and the act changes category.

It becomes intentional.

And intention introduces something far less comfortable to engage with.

There are two competing interpretations.

The first reads this as a form of defiance. That the act of offering retains value independent of outcome. That the existence of something uncorrupted within the self is proven precisely by its willingness to be given, even into harm.

The second reads it as self-negation. That identity has become entangled with suffering to the point where destruction is no longer avoided, but selected. That the gesture is not strength, but a refinement of collapse.

The piece does not resolve this tension.

Because both readings remain intact.

The line concerning the “devil” introduces another layer. It suggests a self-concept in which most of what exists internally has been shaped, compromised, or adapted for survival. What remains—what is being offered—is framed as the last untouched element. Not because it is strong, but because it has not yet been forced to become anything else.

This elevates the offering beyond emotion.

It becomes symbolic.

The act is no longer “giving affection,” but presenting the only remaining part of the self that has not been altered by necessity.

And once offered—

it cannot be reclaimed without changing what it was.
